snapshot.title: 24-Hour Economy targets 30,000 jobs with pharmaceutical park at Ningo Prampram …Today is deadline for drugmakers to register interest
snapshot.evidenceText: The government has opened registration for pharmaceutical manufacturers to establish operations in the Legon Pharmaceutical Innovation Park (LePIP), a 2,000-acre facility planned at Ningo Prampram in the Greater Accra Region. The project, being developed by the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development (24H+) Authority with the Ghana Infrastructure and Investment Fund (GIIF), is expected to create wealth and an estimated 30,000 jobs, according to the Authority. Companies have until today (October 12) to submit expressions of interest. About 70 per cent of Ghana’s pharmaceutical demand is met through imports, costing the country more than $300 million annually, the call for expressions of interest says. The government has set a target of replacing 50 per cent of imports with locally produced medicines by 2030. The Authority describes LePIP as Ghana’s first integrated pharmaceutical innovation park, designed to make the country a manufacturing and export hub for West Africa and beyond. Under the plan, a special purpose vehicle will provide shared infrastructure, including power, water and steam meeting Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, an effluent treatment plant, cold-chain warehousing and ready-built factory shells. Quality control laboratories, supervised by the University of Ghana, and a research centre focused on tropical diseases will also be provided. Tenants will pay fees or lease charges for these services. Companies producing active pharmaceutical ingredients, generics, vaccines, herbal medicines and diagnostics are eligible. Joint ventures and consortia may apply. Anchor tenants may be offered equity in the special purpose vehicle, subject to final terms. The Authority stresses that the exercise is not a tender and confers no lease, award or equity right. Shortlisted firms will be invited to bilateral discussions from October 26 this year. The UK-funded Ghana Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) Programme is supporting the process.

snapshot.title: Syria issues first letter of credit to Saudi Aramco in 14 years | The Jerusalem Post
snapshot.evidenceText: Syria's central bank said on Sunday it issued its first letter of credit in 14 years to facilitate a petroleum products supply deal between the Syrian Petroleum Company and Saudi Aramco (2222.SE).The bank said the transaction was arranged in coordination with a major US bank, which it did not name, opening a channel to finance oil imports and settle payments through the formal banking system.The move marks a step toward restoring Syria's access to international banking channels following the removal of US sanctions and its designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.Saudi Arabia's energy minister signed three memorandums of understanding with Kuwait, Qatar and Egypt to strengthen energy cooperation, the Saudi state news agency said on Sunday.The agreement with Qatar sets a framework for collaboration in petroleum, natural gas and petrochemicals, including exploring joint opportunities to develop pipelines for transport and exports.Syria no longer classified as state sponsor of terrorismThe United States officially removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism at the end of August. Damascus claimed at the time that the step was the last major impediment for the country to bring in foreign investment.Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shibani told Reuters that the government hoped removing what he called the "last obstacle" would help reconnect Syria to the global financial and economic system and boost investment. "There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed Al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar Al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed Al-Sharaa in December 2024.

representative.title: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real | Roman Britain | The Guardian
representative.author: Dalya Alberge

snapshot.title: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
snapshot.evidenceText: Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore. Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists. The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles. Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said. “It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.” In The Dream of Macsen Wledig , medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power. They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills. There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many. With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance. Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory. “He came back and said ‘well, are these any good?’ I said ‘you’ve got to be kidding me’. He’d found two coins dating from the late 4th century. “It is fascinating to consider that the two coins may be linked to the tale of Macsen Wledig – Magnus Maximus – in the Mabinogion, the Welsh equivalent of the Odyssey.” Merrony is a leading specialist in the Romano-British period. His previous discoveries include two Roman villas, at Ford in Pembrokeshire and at Cutteslowe in Oxfordshire. He identified a Roman road along the southern shoulder of the Preselis in 2022, challenging assumptions that the Romans did not venture far into Wales. His research will appear in Antiqvvs , a quarterly magazine dedicated to archaeology, ancient art and history. Magnus Maximus will also feature in Merrony’s forthcoming book, titled Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus . Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Measuring 180 by 150 metres, the fort is on a slope with a commanding view of the surrounding landscape. It is likely to have held about 500 troops, and its discovery overturns assumptions that the area’s Indigenous Celtic tribe was on peaceful terms with the Roman invaders. It has “a characteristic playing-card form, with rounded corners” and a perpendicular road, Merrony said. Finds at the site so far include an unusual iron stylus, many pottery shards, large quantities of Roman tiles and extensive compacted clay floors, a common feature on Roman military sites. Even rut marks left by wagons have been preserved. The geophysical survey confirmed the presence of a rectangular building in the middle of the enclosure and a larger rectangular building immediately to the south. “This arrangement is consistent with the placement of a headquarters building orientated east and thereby ‘facing the enemy’, and a commander’s house,” Merrony said.

representative.title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama : NPR
representative.author: Bill Chappell

snapshot.title: At least 4 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
snapshot.evidenceText: A driver look at his overturned truck in a flooded parking lot on Saturday morning in Tiger Point, Fla., close to where Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday night. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage and power outages wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least four people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed. Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland. One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office. "The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email. A person also died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a room, according to Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons. Four others were hospitalized in the same incident. Many people use generators when they lose connection to the electricity grid. An uprooted tree is seen in Gulf Breeze, Fla., on Saturday. The southeastern U.S. faced a high risk of flooding as Isaias, weakened from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone, moved northward. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham. "We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence." A fourth death was confirmed by Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey's office, which told NPR that a person died in Barbour County, southeast of Montgomery. They did not provide details about the circumstances. More than 390,000 people across the state and Florida were without power as of Sunday morning. At least 95% of outages across the state are expected to be restored by midnight, Alabama Power said on Sunday. In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference. The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners. "Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges. Hurricane Isaias forced a Waffle House restaurant to shut down when it passed through Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane. Joe Raedle/Getty Images hide caption Florida Power & Light Company said it hopes to have power restored to 95% of those impacted by Isaias by end of day Monday. Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin. Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama. "Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service." But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as the Florida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast. On Sunday, there were tornado warnings in North Carolina, as well as high risk of flooding. Other parts of the rest of the East Coast, including Virginia, also saw heavy rain. NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. snapshot.title: Why Saudi airport attacks matter for Bangladesh
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The latest wave of attacks on Saudi airports has killed two Bangladeshis and forced Biman Bangladesh Airlines to suspend its Dhaka-Riyadh flight, bringing the escalating security threat closer to home for Bangladeshis travelling to the kingdom for work and pilgrimage. Saudi Arabian civil aviation authority said 12 people, including two Bangladeshis, were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10. The identities of the two Bangladeshis could not be immediately established. Besides, four Bangladeshis are receiving treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a hospital in Riyadh after the attack, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said today. This attack, the third on Riyadh airport within a week, damaged airport facilities and prompted a temporary suspension of operations, with flights cancelled or diverted. Biman announced on Saturday that its Dhaka-Riyadh-Dhaka flights BG339 and BG340 had been suspended until further notice, citing the suspension of inbound flights at the Riyadh airport. The disruption has also affected other airlines operating between Dhaka and Riyadh. According to CAAB figures reported by Prothom Alo, several flights operated by Saudia and Riyadh Air were cancelled by Sunday morning following the closure of the airport in Riyadh. A US-Bangla Airlines flight was also reported to have diverted on Saturday, arriving in Dhaka early Sunday. For Bangladesh, any prolonged disruption in such a major hub as Riyadh could have wide-ranging consequences. Saudi Arabia is a major destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers, while Jeddah and Madinah are key gateways for those travelling for Umrah and, during the Hajj season, the annual pilgrimage. The demand is reflected in figures cited by the Bangladesh Civil Aviation in August, when its chair said around 1.1 million Bangladeshis travelled to Saudi Arabia through indirect routes. The reference period for the figure was not specified. The two countries also agreed in August to increase direct passenger flights from 49 to 84 a week, reflecting efforts to expand capacity in this corridor. These are permitted flight frequencies, and not the number of flights actually operated. Nonetheless, it reflects the growing traffic on this vital route. Saudi Arabia was Bangladesh's largest source of remittance in the 2025-26 fiscal year, with inflows of $5.85 billion, up from $4.26 billion the previous year, according to Bangladesh Bank. Although remittances do not represent airline revenue, the figures are important as they underline the economic importance of maintaining connectivity between the two countries. Many of the journeys to Saudi Arabia are tied to employment commitments, visa conditions, and prepaid accommodation arrangements. Connectivity delays or flight cancellations could create additional difficulties for passengers with limited flexibility as regards their travel plans. The security threat has also expanded to eastern Saudi Arabia, where the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported that a projectile landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam late Saturday. Coalition spokesman Major General Turki Al-Maliki confirmed the incident. The development is significant for Bangladesh because Dammam is another destination served by Biman and used by travellers heading to Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. snapshot.title: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says | The National
snapshot.evidenceText: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

snapshot.title: Bangladesh seeks removal of Indian export barriers, anti-dumping duties - Sarabangla English
snapshot.evidenceText: Bangladesh has urged India to remove restrictions on Bangladeshi exports, including land port-related barriers and non-tariff obstacles, and withdraw anti-dumping duties imposed on Bangladeshi products. The issues were raised at the 16th meeting of the Bangladesh-India Joint Working Group on Trade, held in New Delhi on October 8–9. The two-day meeting focused on easing bilateral trade barriers, improving land port facilities and strengthening regional connectivity. Bangladesh called for a review of restrictions affecting the entry of its goods into the Indian market, as well as the removal of anti-dumping duties on jute products and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film. It also sought continued tariff preferences for Bangladeshi exports to India after the country graduates from the least developed country (LDC) category. The Bangladeshi delegation emphasised improving market access, harmonising product standards and simplifying certification procedures, including requirements under the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). Dhaka also proposed expanding the movement of goods to Nepal and Bhutan through Indian territory to facilitate regional trade. Improving infrastructure at Indian land customs stations, including warehouses, parking areas, inspection facilities and quarantine services, was another priority. India, meanwhile, raised restrictions affecting the export of cotton yarn and other products to Bangladesh, particularly through designated land ports. The two sides also discussed rail connectivity, border haats and measures to reduce the time and cost of cross-border trade. The 10-member Bangladeshi delegation was led by Ayesha Akter, additional secretary at the Ministry of Commerce. representative.title: ACLU Statement on President Trump’s Latest Attack on the International Criminal Court | American Civil Liberties Union

snapshot.title: ACLU Statement on President Trump’s Latest Attack on the International Criminal Court | American Civil Liberties Union
snapshot.evidenceText: NEW YORK - Today, the Trump administration announced sanctions on the entire International Criminal Court, only hours after one of the court’s former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize. Previously, the United States had sanctioned specific ICC officials, a UN human rights expert, and three Palestinian human rights groups. The international community, including the United States, established the ICC in 1998 to help maintain international peace and security. The ICC investigates and prosecutes atrocity crimes when domestic legal systems are unwilling or unable to do so. 125 countries have joined the international treaty creating the ICC, known as the “Rome Statute.” While the United States has not ratified the Rome Statute, it has supported the ICC’s critical work on a wide range of matters under both Democratic and Republican administrations. “The Trump administration's continued attempts to dismantle the International Criminal Court are disastrous for global justice and human rights accountability,” said Jamil Dakwar, director of the ACLU's Human Rights Program. “We condemn the latest sanctions, which could undercut the ICC's ability to investigate and prosecute atrocities such as genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes, and make it even harder for survivors to get justice. We cannot move backwards and let the Trump administration take the world further down a path of impunity and injustice." The ACLU represents two U.S. human rights advocates in a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump’s initial sanctions targeting the ICC on Feb. 6, 2025. As the lawsuit explains, the sanctions violate the First Amendment by prohibiting the advocates, and other Americans like them, from communicating with the ICC, including by providing legal advice, expert analysis, and evidence. In August, the ACLU and 10 other civil liberties and human rights organizations belonging to the International Network of Civil Liberties Organizations (INCLO) called on the European Commission to protect individuals and organizations targeted by U.S. ICC sanctions from their extra-territorial reach by immediately activating the Council of Europe Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 (‘the Blocking Statute’).

representative.title: IMF warns of AI 'tsunami’ for job seekers
representative.author: Anniek Bao

snapshot.title: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
snapshot.evidenceText: BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training. snapshot.title: Largest 2D map of the universe helps scientists discover new gravitational lenses - Science Tech Updates
snapshot.evidenceText: Using data from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, with help from artificial intelligence, an international team of scientists has discovered 70 new gravitational lenses—rare cosmic alignments that act as natural magnifying glasses. The new lenses further expand one of the largest collections of confirmed lenses to date and will allow scientists to study dark matter, galaxy evolution and the structure of the universe. In August 2026, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team released the largest 2D map of the universe ever created. The 5.6-trillion-pixel map contains nearly 4 billion celestial objects, including stars, galaxies, black holes and asteroids. This map was created using data from three ground-based sky surveys: The Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS) was conducted using the 570-megapixel Department of Energy (DOE)–fabricated Dark Energy Camera (DECam), mounted on the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at NSF Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile, a program of NSF NOIRLab. The Mayall z-band Legacy Survey (MzLS) was conducted using the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO) in Arizona, a program of NSF NOIRLab. The Beijing-Arizona Sky Survey (BASS) at the University of Arizona’s Steward Observatory was conducted with the UA Bok 2.3-meter Telescope at KPNO and supplemented by years of data from NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) satellite mission. From candidates to confirmed lenses The Legacy Surveys map has been 13 years in the making, and regular data releases from the team have enabled scientists to make countless discoveries across a range of subfields in astronomy and astrophysics. In one such research project, an international team led by Xiaosheng Huang (Santa Clara University and DOE’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory) used machine learning to inspect the vast Legacy Surveys data set and identify thousands of new gravitational lens candidates. In an extensive follow-up study published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, led by Emerald Lin (an undergraduate student at UC Berkeley) and Ivonne Toro Bertolla (a research assistant at NSF NOIRLab and science operations assistant at Las Campanas Observatory), the team spectroscopically confirmed 70 of the candidates, establishing them as true instances of gravitational lensing. Cosmic alignments magnify distant objects A gravitational lens occurs when a massive object such as a galaxy, galaxy cluster or black hole lies directly between Earth and a more distant background object. The foreground object’s gravity bends and magnifies the background light, producing arcs, rings and even multiple images of the same object. These natural telescopes allow astronomers to study objects that would otherwise be too distant or faint to detect. They can magnify galaxies from the early universe, reveal the presence and distribution of invisible dark matter, help improve measurements of the universe’s expansion rate and enable the detection of exoplanets—planets orbiting other stars. AI narrows the search “The DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys’ deep and wide-field images have provided an unprecedented foundation for discovering new gravitational lenses,” says Aleksandar Cikota, an associate scientist at NSF NOIRLab, co-author of the study and PI of the follow-up observing program. “What we’re building now is a carefully confirmed sample that researchers can use for years to come.” While the Legacy Surveys provided the foundation for discovering these lenses, that foundation was vast. This created both an opportunity and a challenge: Thousands of gravitational lenses were likely waiting to be found, but visually searching for them was impractical. So the team had to devise a robust and efficient process for scouring the data to identify the lenses buried within them. This is where they turned to artificial intelligence. Using a residual neural network—a form of machine learning designed to recognize subtle patterns in images—the team searched the survey data for the distinctive signatures of gravitational lensing. Earlier work using these techniques had created a catalog containing about 3,500 potential lenses. The machine-learning approach dramatically accelerated the discovery process, allowing astronomers to focus valuable telescope time on follow-up observations of the most promising candidates. “The combination of large surveys and AI-powered searches is transforming how we discover rare objects in the sky,” says Cikota. “These tools allow us to systematically search for systems that, previously, only a few years ago, we might have discovered only serendipitously.” The initial lens searches also relied on advanced computing resources, including infrastructure provided by the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science user facility, underscoring how modern astronomy increasingly depends on powerful computation alongside telescopes. Spectroscopy confirms 70 lenses The AI-powered search uncovered 76 gravitational lens candidates, but this was only the first step. To determine whether an object is truly a gravitational lens, astronomers must use telescopes to measure the distances to both the lensing and background objects. To confirm the lens candidates uncovered in the Legacy Surveys, the team used the Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) instrument on the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope. MUSE was particularly handy for this task since it employs a technique called integral field spectroscopy. Unlike a traditional spectrograph, which records light from only a narrow region of the sky, an integral field spectrograph collects a spectrum at every point across an image. The result is a three-dimensional data set containing both spatial and spectral information. MUSE proved valuable for this study as it allowed the researchers to simultaneously study the lensing and background objects, as well as other nearby objects, in the same observation. The instrument’s broad wavelength coverage also enabled the detection of faint spectral features that revealed the distances and physical properties of the objects involved. Using MUSE observations collected between 2022 and 2024, the team confirmed that 70 of the candidates were true gravitational lenses. A growing resource for cosmic studies While the newly confirmed lenses are scientifically interesting on their own, their greatest impact may come from what they enable in the future. The newly discovered gravitational lenses have been added to the DESI Strong Lens Foundry Project, one of the largest collections of confirmed lenses to date. The large, well-characterized lens sample provides an essential foundation for studies of dark matter, galaxy structure and cosmology. Combined with observations from facilities like the Hubble Space Telescope, the James Webb Space Telescope and the recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, as well as with large surveys like NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), these lenses will help researchers probe the distribution of dark matter, study distant galaxies and test models of cosmic evolution. The work also highlights the enduring scientific value of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. What began as a massive imaging campaign to create a 3D map of the universe is now serving as the foundation for a growing catalog of gravitational lenses that will support discoveries for years to come. “Each confirmed lens adds to a resource that will benefit the entire astronomical community,” says Cikota. “Together, we are building a powerful foundation for future discoveries.” https://noirlab.edu/public/blog/desi-legacy-imaging-surveys/ Scitechupdates.com is a participant in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program, other affiliate and advertising programs, designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees to support the running of this educational site.

snapshot.title: Intensive breathwork reduces brain blood flow and alters neural communication
snapshot.evidenceText: Intensive breathing exercises can reduce blood flow to the brain by up to 45% and alter communication between brain networks, according to a new brain-imaging study. Participants reported experiences resembling some effects of psychedelic drugs, including altered perception, vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity and changes in self-experience. The researchers, presenting the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich, say changes in brain communication, rather than reduced blood flow alone, appear to be key to the altered state. The study involved 30 healthy, experienced breathwork practitioners who performed high-ventilation breathwork during MRI scanning. Participants reported strong altered states of consciousness, describing a predominantly oceanic state – in other words, a deep feeling of connection to the universe - resembling that of a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin, albeit with less pronounced visual effects. Brain imaging showed that global grey-matter cerebral blood flow fell by around 45% during the session, on average from 16.24 to 9.81 ml/100g/min. Those who reported stronger altered states also showed greater changes in the brain's default mode network, which is involved in self-reflection and self-related thinking. The researchers suggest that the intensity of the experience is not simply explained by reduced blood flow. Instead, the experience might track more closely with changes in communication within the default mode network, a brain system linked to self-reflection and self-related thought. Lead researcher Dr Christian Schmitz, Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim in Germany, said: " Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate". 'Co-Coordinator, Hana Adolphi said, " Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness. Understanding these mechanisms could also help inform future research into novel approaches for mental health treatment.
